lessons.title: Lesson 1: Five principles for AI in schools
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: State five responsible-AI principles and apply them to a school example.
This lesson builds toward: Given an AI use in your school, you will apply five responsible-AI principles to it, with one sentence on how it meets or fails each principle.
Most responsible-AI frameworks share a few ideas. Five that fit schools: Human oversight: educators make decisions about students; AI informs, never decides. Fairness and equity: AI should not disadvantage any group of students, and should widen access. Privacy and security: collect and share as little student data as possible, and protect it.
Transparency: students, staff and families know when and how AI is used. Accountability: a named person owns each AI tool and its effects, and there is a way to raise concerns.
These match the principles in the US Department of Education's July 22, 2025 Dear Colleague Letter on AI, which, as reported by K-12 Dive, calls for AI initiatives that are educator-led, ethical, accessible to students with disabilities, transparent in rollout and compliant with federal privacy laws. For risk management, NIST's voluntary AI Risk Management Framework (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage) is a free reference.
Words to know:
- Human oversight: people reviewing and deciding, with AI only informing.
- Equity: making sure every student gets what they need to succeed.
- Transparency: being open about when and how AI is used.
Official sources:
- K-12 Dive: Education Department issues AI priorities (July 2025)
- NIST AI Risk Management Framework
Try it now: Take one AI use in your school (for example, an adaptive reading program). Write one sentence on how it meets or fails each of the five principles.
You can now apply five responsible-AI principles to a real school use.

check.q: What does the transparency principle mean?
options: Being open about when and how AI is used
Using only free AI tools
Letting AI make decisions in public
Sharing student data with families
check.why: Transparency means people know when and how AI is used.

check.q: An adaptive reading program chooses each student's next book. Which principle question would you ask?
options: Is it the cheapest program?
Is it the newest program?
Can teachers see its choices and change them?
Does it have the most features?
check.why: Human oversight means educators decide and AI informs.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Bias and equity risks in school AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Spot where school AI uses could treat groups of students unfairly.
This lesson builds toward: Given an AI tool that scores, flags or adapts to students, you will identify where it could treat groups of students unfairly, writing three equity questions for the vendor and one check on your own results.
AI learns from data, and data reflects the past, including unfairness. In schools, watch four places. Detectors: AI-writing detectors can wrongly flag honest work, and English learners' writing may be flagged more often. Prediction: early-warning or risk scores can label students based on patterns linked to income, disability or race.
Tracking: adaptive programs that keep giving some students easier work can narrow their opportunities. Access: if AI help needs a device or home internet, students without them fall further behind; if a tool is not accessible, students with disabilities are shut out.
Equity checks: ask vendors how they test for bias and accessibility; look at results by student group in your own data (with privacy protections); never use an AI score alone for placement, discipline or eligibility decisions; and make sure every student can reach the tool at school.
Step by step:
- List AI uses that sort, score or flag students.
- Ask the vendor how it tests for bias and accessibility.
- Review results by student group, protecting privacy.
- Never use an AI score alone for decisions about students.
- Check every student can access the tool at school.
Words to know:
- Algorithmic bias: unfair results from an AI system, often learned from past data.
- Risk score: a number a system gives a student to predict a problem, like dropping out.
- Tracking: keeping students on different levels of work, which can limit opportunities.
Try it now: Choose one AI tool that scores, flags or adapts to students in your school. Write three equity questions you would ask the vendor and one check you would run on your own results.
You can now spot equity risks in school AI and put practical checks in place.

check.q: Why can AI-writing detectors raise equity concerns?
options: They are too expensive
They may flag English learners' writing more often
They work only on phones
They grade too slowly
check.why: Unequal false flags fall on some groups of students more than others.

check.q: An adaptive tool keeps one group of students on easier work for months. What would you do?
options: Nothing; the tool knows best
Turn off all AI in the school
Move those students to another school
Check your own results by group and ask the vendor how the tool decides
check.why: Checking results by group shows whether the tool narrows opportunity for some students.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Privacy and security: FERPA, COPPA and good habits
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Apply FERPA and COPPA and basic security habits to AI tools.
This lesson builds toward: When staff use AI tools, you will apply FERPA, COPPA and basic security habits, with five plain-language habits, each with an example of what not to do.
FERPA protects student education records. Schools generally need consent to disclose personally identifiable information from them, with exceptions; a vendor may act as a school official only if it performs a school service, is under the school's direct control, and follows limits on re-sharing. Parents can inspect and review records; rights move to students at 18 or in college.
COPPA, enforced by the FTC, protects children under 13 online. The FTC says schools may consent for parents only when information is collected for the school's use and benefit and for no other commercial purpose. The FTC amended its COPPA Rule on April 22, 2025; check the FTC's pages for current requirements.
Good habits: data minimization (share only what the task needs), approved tools only, district accounts with strong passwords and two-step sign-in, no uploading of records to personal accounts, and knowing who to call if data may have leaked. Your state may have its own student-privacy law; your privacy officer will know.
Step by step:
- Use only approved tools for student information.
- Share the minimum data needed.
- Use district accounts with two-step sign-in.
- Never upload records to personal accounts.
- Know who to call about a possible leak.
Words to know:
- Data minimization: collecting and sharing only the data a task really needs.
- Two-step sign-in: logging in with a password plus a second check, like a code on your phone.
Official sources:
- FERPA: Protecting Student Privacy
- FTC: Complying with COPPA, Frequently Asked Questions
Try it now: Write five privacy and security habits for your staff in plain words, with one example of what NOT to do for each.
You can now apply FERPA, COPPA and everyday security habits to staff use of AI.

options: A second check, such as a code on your phone
A second password typed twice
A second AI tool
A second staff member to sign in for you
check.why: A second check protects accounts even if a password is stolen.

check.q: A teacher wants to upload a whole class list to an AI tool for one small task. What would you advise?
options: Upload it; more data gives better results
Upload it to two tools to compare
Share only what the task needs, in an approved tool
Email it to the vendor instead
check.why: Data minimization means sharing only what the task needs.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Vetting vendors and agreements
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Run a vendor review before an AI tool is approved.
This lesson builds toward: Before an AI tool is approved, you will run a vendor review from the tool's public documents, listing what the vendor must confirm in a signed agreement.
Every AI tool that will touch student information needs a review before approval. Use the Student Privacy Policy Office's Model Terms of Service checklist or your district's own. Key questions: what data, who owns it, is it used for advertising or to train AI, can it be deleted on request, who else receives it, how is it secured, and what happens in a breach.
Add AI-specific questions: How does the AI work and what are its limits? How is it tested for accuracy, bias and accessibility? Can teachers see and override its outputs? Does it keep student inputs, and for how long?
Get commitments in a signed agreement, not just a website policy that can change. Many states and districts use data privacy agreements with vendors; your privacy officer or counsel will know the right form.
Step by step:
- Use the Model Terms of Service checklist or your district's.
- Ask the AI-specific questions.
- Request written answers.
- Get commitments in a signed agreement.
- Record the decision and review date.
Words to know:
- Data privacy agreement: a signed contract setting how a vendor may use and protect student data.
- Override: a person changing or rejecting what the AI produced.
Official sources:
- Privacy and Education Technology: Model Terms of Service checklist
Try it now: Run a vendor review on one AI tool your school uses or wants: answer the privacy and AI questions from its public documents, and list what you would need the vendor to confirm in writing.
You can now review an AI vendor on privacy, AI quality and contract terms before approval.

check.q: What is a data privacy agreement?
options: A vendor's marketing page
A signed contract on how a vendor uses and protects student data
A form students sign
A list of approved websites
check.why: A signed agreement holds the vendor to its commitments.

check.q: A vendor's website says it never trains AI on student data. What would you do?
options: Approve the tool on that basis
Ignore it
Ask students if it is true
Get that commitment in the signed agreement
check.why: Website policies can change; a signed agreement does not change on its own.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Writing responsible-AI guidelines
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Draft clear guidelines for staff and student AI use.
This lesson builds toward: With input from teachers, students and families, you will draft responsible-AI guidelines with may and may-not rules for staff and students, with at least four concrete items each, checked against district policy and state law with counsel.
Guidelines turn principles into everyday rules. Keep them to about two pages and use plain words. Sections: purpose and principles; approved tools and how to request a new one; privacy rules; what staff may and may not do; what students may and may not do (link your AI use levels); academic integrity; transparency with families; and who to contact.
Use concrete examples: "Staff may use approved AI tools to draft lesson materials and family letters. Staff may not enter student names, grades, IEP or 504 information, or discipline records into any unapproved tool. Staff may not use AI to make grading, placement or discipline decisions."
Write them with teachers, students (age-appropriately) and families, check them with counsel against district policy and state law, and set a review date. Guidelines nobody helped write are guidelines nobody follows.
Step by step:
- Draft the sections: principles, tools, privacy, staff, students, integrity, transparency, contact.
- Add concrete may / may not examples.
- Involve teachers, students and families.
- Check with counsel against policy and state law.
- Publish and set a review date.
Words to know:
- Guidelines: practical rules that explain how to follow a policy day to day.
- Board policy: a formal rule adopted by the school board.
Try it now: Draft the staff and student "may / may not" sections of your guidelines with at least four items each. Share them with two teachers and note their changes.
You can now write practical responsible-AI guidelines with the people who will follow them.

check.q: What makes guidelines useful to staff?
options: Concrete may and may-not examples
Long legal language
A list of every AI tool on the market
No examples, so staff can decide
check.why: Concrete examples make rules easy to follow.

check.q: Your draft guidelines are ready. What should happen before they are adopted?
options: Post them right away
Ask an AI chatbot to approve them
Get teacher, student and family input and check them against policy and law with counsel
Keep them secret from staff
check.why: Guidelines need input from the people affected and a legal check.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: When something goes wrong: incident response
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Plan the steps for an AI incident, including data leaks and deepfakes.
This lesson builds toward: Given a realistic AI incident such as a deepfake or data leak, you will walk through a six-step incident response plan, starting with making the student safe and ending with updating the guidelines.
Plan before the incident. Common AI incidents: student data entered into an unapproved tool; an AI tool giving harmful or wrong information to students; and AI-generated fake images, audio or video of students or staff (deepfakes), which can be harassment and may be a crime.
A six-step plan: 1) Make safe: stop the harm (remove access, pause the tool, support the affected person). 2) Report: to the principal and the district contact named in your guidelines. 3) Preserve: keep evidence as your district directs (for images of minors, follow law-enforcement and counsel guidance; never forward or copy them). 4) Assess: what data or people are affected. 5) Notify: families and others as law and policy require. 6) Learn: fix the cause and update guidelines.
For deepfakes and harassment, follow your bullying, harassment and Title IX procedures and involve counsel and, where required, law enforcement. Laws on AI-generated images are changing quickly at federal and state level; your counsel will know what applies.
Step by step:
- Make safe: stop the harm and support the person.
- Report to the principal and district contact.
- Preserve evidence as directed; never forward images of minors.
- Assess what data or people are affected.
- Notify as law and policy require; then learn and update.
Words to know:
- Incident response: the planned steps for handling something that went wrong.
- Deepfake: a fake image, voice or video made with AI to look real.
- Title IX: the federal law against sex discrimination in education, including sexual harassment.
Try it now: Final task: finish your two-page responsible-AI guidelines (principles, privacy, equity, staff and student rules, vendor steps, six-step incident plan). Test them by reviewing one real tool and walking through one realistic incident, noting any gap you found.
You can now lead responsible AI in your school with clear guidelines, vendor review and an incident plan.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Principles Fewer than five principles, or they are not in plain words. Five principles in plain words. Each principle has a short school example. Privacy and equity Privacy rules or equity checks are missing. Privacy rules (FERPA, COPPA, approved tools only) and equity checks are included. Equity checks say how the school will look at its own results by group. Staff and student rules No may and may-not rules, or they are vague. Says what staff and students may and may not do. Teachers reviewed the rules and their changes were made. Vendor review No vendor steps, or no real tool was reviewed. Vendor review steps, tested on one real AI tool. Lists what the vendor must confirm in a signed agreement. Incident plan Fewer than six steps, or not tested on an incident. A six-step incident plan, walked through on one realistic incident. Notes a gap found in the walk-through and how the guidelines will change. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What is the last step of the incident plan?
options: Make safe
Learn: fix the cause and update the guidelines
Notify the press
Delete all records
check.why: Learning from each incident keeps it from happening again.

check.q: A staff member receives an AI fake image of a student. What should they do with it?
options: Forward it to colleagues so they know
Post a warning with the image
Delete it and say nothing
Not forward it, and follow counsel and law-enforcement guidance on preserving evidence
check.why: Images of minors are never forwarded; evidence is handled as counsel and law enforcement advise.
